subject: Nanotechnology
title: What Is Self-Assembly
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on What Is Self-Assembly.

hook.text: Snowflakes, cell membranes, and virus shells all build themselves — no instruction manual, no factory, just physics.

buildup.text: Self-assembly means components spontaneously organize into ordered structures driven by local interactions.

discovery.text: The driving forces are non-covalent: hydrogen bonds, van der Waals forces, hydrophobic effects, and electrostatics.

twist.text: Unlike top-down manufacturing, self-assembly works from the bottom up — no tools touch the product at all.

climax.text: Nanotechnologists harness self-assembly to build structures too small for any machine to fabricate directly.

punchline.text: Nature builds without hands — self-assembly is manufacturing by physics.

quiz.question: What drives self-assembly at the nanoscale?
options: External robotic manipulation of individual atoms
Non-covalent forces like hydrogen bonds, van der Waals, and hydrophobic interactions
